subChunks.title: Standards, Guardrails & Evolving Architecture Across Teams
subChunks.hookHtml: Architecture governance is how you maintain architectural coherence as teams grow, services multiply, and people move on. Without it, every team makes independent choices that are locally sensible but globally incoherent — five different logging libraries, three authentication patterns, and APIs that work completely differently. With it, the system remains navigable and the architecture can be evolved deliberately.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
What Architecture Governance Is

Architecture governance is the set of processes, standards, and review mechanisms that ensure technical decisions align with the overall architectural direction — across teams, over time, at scale. It is not a committee that blocks work. It is a framework that enables teams to make good decisions independently, with enough guidance to stay aligned without needing approval for everything.

Architecture Standards

Standards define the agreed ways of doing common things: how services expose APIs, what logging format is used, how configuration is managed, what authentication mechanism is required. Standards reduce cognitive overhead (engineers don't have to redecide every choice) and make the system coherent (any engineer can navigate any service).

Effective standards are: specific enough to be actionable, documented in one canonical place, versioned when they change, and enforced automatically where possible (linters, CI checks, templates).

Ineffective standards are: aspirational but not enforced, out of date, scattered across wikis, or so prescriptive they prevent sensible exceptions.

Guardrails vs Gates

Gates: mandatory approval before you can proceed. Slow. Create bottlenecks. Use for genuinely irreversible, high-risk decisions only (external API contracts, security-critical systems).

Guardrails: automated checks and templates that guide decisions in the right direction without requiring approval. Fast. Scale infinitely. Use for everything else: architecture decision templates, CI checks for API conformance, security scanning, standardised service scaffolding.

The goal: make the right thing the easy thing. A scaffold that produces a correctly-structured service with all standards pre-wired is more effective than a review process that checks for those standards after the fact.

Architecture Review Boards (ARB)

An Architecture Review Board is a forum (not a veto committee) for reviewing significant design decisions. Effective ARBs: meet regularly (weekly or bi-weekly), review concrete proposals (RFC, ADR draft) not abstract ideas, focus on 'how can we make this work' not 'should we approve this', and publish decisions with rationale for the whole organisation.

Signs of an ineffective ARB: every decision requires ARB approval (bottleneck), the ARB doesn't review decisions until after they are already implemented (theatre), or the ARB rejects work without explaining the standard that was violated.

Evolving Architecture Across Teams

Large architectural changes (migrating from monolith to services, changing the authentication pattern, adopting a new messaging system) cannot be done by one team in one sprint. They require: a clear migration path, a working example that other teams can copy, tooling support (libraries, scaffolding), a timeline with reasonable transition periods, and agreement on the end state.

The strangler fig pattern: new functionality built with the new pattern; old functionality gradually migrated as it needs to change. No big-bang rewrites. The old and new coexist during the transition.

storyBeats.text: The Academy grew from three engineers to forty. Within a year, the system had six different patterns for handling database transactions, four logging formats, three service authentication methods, and two incompatible approaches to error handling. No single engineer could navigate any service outside their own team. Incidents took twice as long to diagnose because every service needed to be learned from scratch.

storyBeats.speaker: Head of Architecture Nen
storyBeats.text: Architecture governance is not about control — it is about reducing the tax that every engineer pays every time they encounter a service built by a different team. When we agree that all services log JSON with the same field names, any engineer can search any service's logs without learning a new format. That is a compounding efficiency gain that grows with every engineer you hire.

storyBeats.speaker: Head of Architecture Nen
storyBeats.text: The failure mode of governance is making it a gate rather than a guardrail. If teams need ARB approval to use a new library, engineers will work around the ARB, the ARB will become a backlog, and the system will be incoherent anyway. Instead: make the good library the default in your service template, make the bad one trigger a CI warning. The decision is made by the path of least resistance.

storyBeats.speaker: Head of Architecture Nen
storyBeats.text: Evolving the architecture of a live system with forty teams is not a sprint. It is a migration. The strangler fig pattern is the only thing that works at scale: build the new way, demonstrate it, give teams a scaffold to copy, and let the old way die as things naturally get touched. Set a sunset date for the old pattern, not an immediate cutover. Big-bang migrations are almost always a disaster.

learningObjectives: Distinguish between architecture gates (approval-required) and guardrails (automated guidance) and explain when each is appropriate
Describe the elements of an effective Architecture Review Board and identify signs of an ineffective one
Explain the strangler fig pattern for evolving architecture across teams without big-bang migrations
Write an architecture standard that is specific, actionable, and enforceable
commonMistakes: Making every architectural decision require ARB approval — creates a bottleneck that teams route around
Documenting standards without automating their enforcement — standards drift without CI checks and templates
Planning big-bang architectural migrations — strangler fig pattern is safer and more practical
Allowing the ARB to review decisions after they are implemented — governance theatre that changes nothing
assessmentCriteria: Can give an example of converting an architecture gate into a guardrail for a given standard
Can describe the strangler fig migration pattern and explain why it is preferable to big-bang for cross-team changes
Can identify three signs of an ineffective ARB and propose concrete improvements
Can write an architecture standard with correct elements: specific behaviour, rationale, how it is enforced, exception process
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain architecture governance to an engineering manager who thinks it means 'a committee that slows teams down.' What does good governance actually look like? What does it enable? How is a guardrail different from a gate?
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Answer the following governance scenarios:

  1. You discover that four teams each implemented their own HTTP client wrapper with different retry logic, timeout settings, and error handling. How do you fix this going forward without blocking any team's current work?
  2. Your ARB currently requires approval before any team creates a new service. The review takes 2 weeks and most requests are approved. What would you change and why?
  3. You need to migrate all services from basic auth to JWT across 12 teams over 6 months. Write the migration plan at a high level, specifying: what the teams get on day 1, what the transition period looks like, and what happens at the end.
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
1. Four different HTTP client wrappers:
   Fix going forward (not blocking current work):
   a) Build a canonical HttpClient library with standard retry (exponential backoff + jitter), timeouts (connect 2s, read 10s configurable), structured error handling, and correlation ID propagation. Include it in the service scaffold.
   b) Declare it the standard in the architecture decisions record.
   c) Add a CI advisory (not a blocker) when a new HTTP client wrapper is detected (grep for common wrapper patterns).
   d) Deprecate the four existing wrappers — teams migrate their own wrappers as they touch those services (strangler fig). Set a sunset date (6 months).
   e) Do NOT require teams to immediately migrate — that is a bottleneck and they're working. Migration happens as natural work touches those services.

2. ARB approval bottleneck:
   Issues: 2-week approval for every new service means 2 weeks of blocked team velocity, and if most are approved, the review is low-value for most cases.
   Changes:
   - Convert to a guardrail: provide a service creation scaffold/template that auto-implements all standards (auth, logging, health endpoint, CI). Creating a service from the scaffold does NOT require ARB review.
   - Reserve ARB review for genuinely novel architecture decisions: new messaging patterns, new data persistence technology, cross-team API contracts. These should be rare.
   - Publish a 'pre-approved patterns' list — teams using these patterns need no approval at all.
   - Change ARB cadence: weekly, async-first (RFC posted 3 days before), approval via comment not meeting.

3. Basic auth → JWT migration across 12 teams:
   Day 1 — teams receive:
   - A JWT library with a standard implementation (issue/validate tokens), full documentation, examples
   - A migration guide: 'here is how to replace basic auth with JWT in 3 steps'
   - A reference implementation in the spell-service (already migrated by the platform team)

   Transition period (months 1–5):
   - Both auth patterns accepted — no team is blocked
   - Each team adds JWT support alongside existing basic auth on their own schedule
   - Platform team available for pairing/support
   - Dashboard showing migration status per service (complete/in-progress/not-started)
   - Monthly review of progress in architecture sync

   End state (month 6):
   - Sunset date: basic auth rejected at the API gateway (returns 401 with clear message) for all services
   - Any team not migrated by month 5 gets a dedicated migration sprint with platform team support
   - Basic auth library deprecated in maven bom after sunset
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Write an architecture standard for the Academy's service APIs. The standard should cover: (1) URL naming conventions (2) HTTP method usage (3) Error response format (4) Authentication requirement (5) Required headers. For each: state the rule specifically, give a compliant example, give a non-compliant example, and state how it is enforced. End with the exception process.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
# Academy API Standards — v2.1 (2026-05)

1. URL Naming:
   Rule: plural nouns, kebab-case, no verbs in URLs. Resources are addressable by ID.
   Compliant: GET /api/spells, GET /api/spells/{id}, POST /api/spell-casts
   Non-compliant: GET /api/getSpell, POST /api/castSpell, GET /api/Spell
   Enforcement: CI lint (OpenAPI spec validation, regex check on route definitions)

2. HTTP Methods:
   Rule: GET (read, idempotent), POST (create), PUT (full replace), PATCH (partial update), DELETE (remove). Never use POST for read operations.
   Compliant: GET /api/spells?tier=SENIOR (search/filter)
   Non-compliant: POST /api/spells/search
   Enforcement: OpenAPI schema validation in CI; PR review checklist item

3. Error Response Format:
   Rule: All 4xx/5xx responses MUST return JSON: {"error": "message", "code": "ERROR_CODE", "requestId": "uuid"}
   Compliant: 400 {"error": "Spell name is required", "code": "VALIDATION_ERROR", "requestId": "abc-123"}
   Non-compliant: 400 "Bad Request" (plain text), 500 with stack trace
   Enforcement: integration test template includes error format assertions; static analysis for raw exception propagation

4. Authentication:
   Rule: All non-public endpoints MUST validate a Bearer JWT in the Authorization header. Public endpoints MUST be explicitly documented with @PublicEndpoint annotation.
   Compliant: Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGc...
   Non-compliant: Basic auth, API key in query param, unauthenticated endpoint with no @PublicEndpoint
   Enforcement: Spring Security filter enforced globally; CI scan for missing @PublicEndpoint on non-secured routes

5. Required Headers:
   Rule: All requests must include X-Request-Id (UUID); all responses must echo it.
   Enforcement: API gateway injects X-Request-Id if absent; service framework propagates via MDC; integration test checks echo

Exception Process:
Teams with a justified reason to deviate must submit an ADR to the architecture Slack channel with 48-hour async review. Approved exceptions are recorded and have a sunset date if temporary.

questions.questionHtml: What is the key difference between an architecture gate and an architecture guardrail?
options: Gates are for security, guardrails are for code style
Gates require manual approval before proceeding; guardrails are automated mechanisms that guide decisions in the right direction without requiring approval
Gates are used in CI; guardrails are used in code review
Gates apply to new services; guardrails apply to existing ones
questions.correctAnswer: Gates require manual approval before proceeding; guardrails are automated mechanisms that guide decisions in the right direction without requiring approval
questions.explanationHtml: Gates are approval-required checkpoints — useful for genuinely irreversible or high-risk decisions, but they create bottlenecks when overused. Guardrails (automated linting, CI checks, standardised scaffolding, pre-approved patterns) guide teams to the right choice without a human approval step. The goal of effective governance is to maximise guardrails and minimise gates, making the correct choice the path of least resistance.

questions.questionHtml: You need to migrate 15 services from REST to an event-driven API pattern over 6 months. Which approach is most appropriate?
options: Schedule a 2-week big-bang migration sprint for all 15 services simultaneously
Use the strangler fig pattern: build new event-driven interfaces alongside existing REST, migrate services gradually, sunset REST endpoints after transition
Pause all feature work until the migration is complete
Require each team to rewrite their service from scratch in the new pattern
questions.correctAnswer: Use the strangler fig pattern: build new event-driven interfaces alongside existing REST, migrate services gradually, sunset REST endpoints after transition
questions.explanationHtml: The strangler fig pattern allows the old and new patterns to coexist during transition — no team is blocked, production is never fully disrupted, and teams can migrate at their own pace within a defined window. Big-bang migrations in a multi-service environment are extremely high-risk: 15 services changing simultaneously means 15 ways the migration can fail simultaneously, with no clean rollback path.

questions.questionHtml: An Architecture Review Board has a 3-week backlog for service creation approvals. Teams are creating services without requesting approval to avoid the wait. What is the root problem?
options: Teams lack discipline — they should wait for approval
The ARB needs more members to process requests faster
The governance model is using gates where guardrails would be more effective — the approval process adds cost without proportionate risk reduction
Service creation should be banned until the backlog clears
questions.correctAnswer: The governance model is using gates where guardrails would be more effective — the approval process adds cost without proportionate risk reduction
questions.explanationHtml: When teams route around a governance process, that is feedback that the process has a design problem. A 3-week approval for routine service creation means teams either wait (losing velocity) or route around it (making governance theatre). The solution is not more enforcement — it is redesign: convert to a guardrail (scaffold, pre-approved patterns, automated conformance checks) so teams can create services instantly while automatically implementing all required standards.
